nameStory: This tiny green algae gets its scientific name from Greek words meaning 'crown ball' - stephanos for crown and sphaira for ball - describing how its flagellated cells arrange themselves in a distinctive crown-like sphere. The species name 'pluvialis' means 'of the rain,' hinting at where you might find this microscopic marvel after a good downpour.
description: Stephanosphaera is a microscopic green algae that forms tiny floating colonies of cells, each equipped with whip-like flagella for swimming. These aren't your typical pond scum - they're organized into elegant spherical colonies that drift through temporary puddles and rain pools. You won't see individual colonies without a microscope, but you might notice a faint greenish tinge in the water where they're abundant. Each colony is smaller than the period at the end of this sentence.

idTips.label: Microscopic colonies
idTips.description: Requires magnification to see - forms tiny spherical colonies of flagellated cells that create a crown-like arrangement

idTips.label: Temporary water bodies
idTips.description: Found in puddles, rain pools, and other temporary water collections rather than permanent ponds or streams

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: May give water a subtle green tint when present in large numbers, but individual colonies are invisible to naked eye

idTips.label: Swimming motion
idTips.description: Under magnification, colonies show active swimming movement due to coordinated flagellar beating

habitat: This rare algae appears in temporary pools of rainwater, puddles, and shallow depressions that collect water after storms in New England. It prefers these ephemeral water bodies over permanent ponds or lakes, thriving in the nutrient-rich conditions of fresh rainwater mixed with organic matter.

seasonality.spring: Most likely to appear in spring rain pools and melting snow puddles when temperatures warm and daylight increases.
seasonality.summer: May be found in temporary puddles after heavy summer rains, though hot weather can quickly evaporate suitable habitat.
seasonality.fall: Can appear in autumn rain pools, especially during wet periods with moderate temperatures.
seasonality.winter: Dormant or absent during freezing conditions when temporary water bodies are frozen solid.

funFact: Despite being a simple algae, Stephanosphaera's cells work together like a microscopic synchronized swimming team - all their whip-like flagella beat in perfect coordination to propel the entire crown-shaped colony through the water!
confusionNotes: Under a microscope, it could be confused with other colonial green algae like Volvox, but Stephanosphaera's distinctive crown-ball arrangement of cells and preference for temporary rain puddles (rather than permanent water bodies) sets it apart.
contextualKnowledge: Though originally classified with the famous Volvox family of colonial algae, genetic studies revealed that Stephanosphaera is actually more closely related to single-celled algae, showing how appearances can be deceiving even in the microscopic world.
compareHints: Stephanosphaera is the only species in its genus, making it unique among New England algae. Within its family (Haematococcaceae), it differs from relatives by forming these distinctive crown-shaped colonies rather than living as single cells. Its closest relative is actually a unicellular algae called Balticola, showing how this species took an evolutionary leap into colonial living.
